name: creachat_threads
description: One moderator's conversation with the AI assistant. The whole exchange lives in one column as a JSON array, because that is the shape every access needs: read the complete thread, append a pair, save.

columns.name: id
columns.description: The thread identifier, chosen by the caller rather than by the database. Legacy stores it as char(36).

columns.name: messages
columns.description: The complete exchange as a JSON array of messages. Nothing ever reads or writes a single message.
columns.note: Legacy uses MySQL longtext. The bound that matters is the model's context window, not the column.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.description: Maintained by the update query, not by an ON UPDATE clause — a column half-owned by the DDL and half by the query is the kind of thing nobody can answer a question about later.

notes: The messages column is a document, not a relation, and that is the design: the Anthropic Messages API is stateless, so every call sends the whole thread anyway. Splitting it into rows would buy nothing and cost a join on every turn.

Because the whole thread is rewritten on every append, two concurrent appends lose one of the two. Legacy has no guard for it. Both implementations need the same one — a version column or a conditional update — or they will disagree about what a thread contains.
The primary key is not generated by the database. An implementation that relies on an autoincrement here will write the wrong thing.
Timestamps are UTC milliseconds; see types/Timestamp.json.
